[MUQATIL:101:7-8/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The light scales belong to shirk: its good deeds become ash scattered by wind, leaving nothing to weigh; it is the foulest thing and the lightest in the balance.
[MUQATIL:101:9-11/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The scales are light because of the person's evil deeds; truth is heavy and wholesome, whereas falsehood is light and vile.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p392#3/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · عبيد بن عمير | reports | Ubayd ibn Umayr says even a huge, tall, voracious man weighs no more than a gnat's wing before God.
[TAB:101:8/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Those whose good deeds weigh little have the Hawiya as their abode, where they fall headfirst in Hell.
[TAB:101:8/r2] TAB, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the Hawiya is the Fire, the sinners' refuge; the phrase can also be an Arabic exclamation for a person in dire trouble.
[TAB:101:8/r3] TAB, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda explains هوت أمه as a familiar Arabic phrase used when someone faces a severe predicament.
[TAB:101:8/r4] TAB, d. 310 · الأشعث بن عبد الله الأعمى | reports | Al-Ashʿath describes believers' spirits welcoming a dead believer from worldly grief; asked about the dead, they say they were taken to their mother, the Hawiya.
[TAB:101:8/r5] TAB, d. 310 · أبو صالح | reports | Abū Ṣāliḥ says they fall headfirst into the Fire.
[TAB:101:8/r6] TAB, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda also says the person falls into the Fire headfirst.
[TAB:101:8/r7] TAB, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd explains that the Fire is called the person's mother because it is his refuge and the place to which he returns. | mentions 3:151
[TAB:101:8/r8] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Fire is made his mother because, with no other home, it shelters him as a woman shelters her child.
[THALABI:v10p274#3/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | For the one whose scales are light, his destination and home are Hell.
[THALABI:v10p274#3/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · قتادة | reports | He says hāwat ummuh is a familiar Arabic expression used when someone falls into a severe predicament.
[THALABI:v10p274#3/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · بعضهم | reports | Some interpret ‘his mother’ as his head, meaning the people fall headfirst into Hell; Qatada and Abu Salih adopted this interpretation.
[THALABI:v10p274#3/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس بن مالك | reports | He reports an angel weighing each person’s deeds; a heavy scale brings a public proclamation of lasting felicity, while a light one brings lasting misery.
[MAWARDI:101:8/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd identifies Hawiya as Hell, called the person's mother because he takes refuge there as a child does with its mother; Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's poem supports the refuge sense.
[MAWARDI:101:8/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Hell is called Hawiya because the person falls into it, though it has a deep abyss.
[MAWARDI:101:8/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima instead reads mother as the person's own head, upon which he falls into Hell; a poem addressed to ʿAmr illustrates this image.
[MAWARDI:101:9/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd identifies Hawiya as Hell, called the person's mother because he takes refuge there as a child does with its mother; Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's poem supports the refuge sense.
[MAWARDI:101:9/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Hell is called Hawiya because the person falls into it, though it has a deep abyss.
[MAWARDI:101:9/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima instead reads mother as the person's own head, upon which he falls into Hell; a poem addressed to ʿAmr illustrates this image.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p444/r11] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Those whose scales are light in acts of obedience are the disbelievers, whose abode is the abyss.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p264/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The person with light scales has evil deeds outweighing his good deeds.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p264/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil similarly says the truth is heavy and falsehood is light.
[BAGHAWI:101:8/r1] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | The one whose scales are light is the one whose evil deeds outweigh the good.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p514/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Light scales mean that a person's evil deeds outweigh the good.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p796/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Mawazin may mean deeds with weight before God or weighing scales; heaviness is their being outweighed.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p796/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · أبو بكر | reports | Abu Bakr told Umar that truth-followers' scales grow heavy through their conduct, while falsehood-followers' grow light; scales holding only good are rightly heavy.
[IBNATIYYA:101:8/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · جمهور العلماء والفقهاء والمحدثين | reports | Most scholars, jurists, and hadith scholars affirm a literal balance on the Resurrection, with a beam, so people can understand divine judgment through a form they know and trust.
[IBNATIYYA:101:8/r2] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid denies a literal balance and takes it as a metaphor for justice, since a scale is the fairest measure known to people.
[IBNATIYYA:101:8/r3] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The plural balances are assigned to a person because that person has many different things to be weighed.
[IBNATIYYA:101:8/r4] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | A balance is heavy through faith and deeds, and light through their absence or scarcity; a believer’s balance will never be disastrously light.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p516#3/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · المؤمن | holds | A believer's balance never becomes ruinously light.
[TABRISI:101:5-11/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Light scales mean few good deeds and little obedience.
[RAZI:101:6/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | On describing the Resurrection, God divides people into two groups according to the heaviness or lightness of their scales.
[RAZI:101:6/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ takes mawāzīn as the plural of mawzūn, meaning a deed with weight and worth before God; he compares it to saying one thing is by the measure or weight of another.
[RAZI:101:6/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās takes the word as balances with a tongue and two pans: obedient people's good deeds appear beautiful and, if they outweigh, lead to Paradise; unbelievers' evil deeds appear ugly and light, leading to the Fire.
[RAZI:101:6/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says the balance has two pans but does not describe it further.
[RAZI:101:6/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · المتكلمون | reports | The theologians say deeds themselves cannot be weighed, especially after ceasing to exist; instead, records may be weighed, light and darkness may signify good and evil, or the records may be embodied beautifully or hideously, publicly revealing people's standing.
[RAZI:101:8/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The scales are light because a person's good deeds are few, so the evil deeds outweigh them.
[RAZI:101:8/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · أبو بكر | reports | Abū Bakr says scales are heavy when people follow truth and bear its weight in worldly life, and light when they follow falsehood and its ease; a scale containing only truth is rightly heavy, one holding falsehood rightly light.
[RAZI:101:8/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil says truth itself is heavy while falsehood is light.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Light scales mean few good deeds, with wrongs outweighing right actions.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو بكر | reports | Abu Bakr says the scale grows heavy through following the weighty truth in life, and grows light through following falsehood.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Al-Razi relays Muqatils explanation that truth is heavy and falsehood light.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The balance has a pan and a tongue on which written records of good and bad deeds are weighed; Qurtubi discussed it under earlier surahs and in his Remembrance book.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | One interpretation says there is a single balance in Gabriel's hand weighing human deeds, expressed in plural form.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another interpretation posits multiple balances, supported by a poet's line about each event having its balance.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عبد العزيز بن يحيى | reports | Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya takes the balances as proofs and arguments, citing a poet who says he had a balance for every disputant.
[BAYDAWI:101:8/r1] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | His scales are light because he has no good deed worthy of consideration.
[BAYDAWI:101:8/r2] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Alternatively, his evil deeds outweigh his good deeds.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:101:1-11/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Light scales mean no worthy good deed exists or evil deeds outweigh good ones.
[NASAFI:101:8/r1] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The balances are light because their owners followed falsehood.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#8/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The scales are light because the person followed falsehood.
[QASHANI:101:1-5/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | This annihilation reading does not fit the later distinction of heavy and light scales; in God’s scale, rising and ascending count as weight, while descent is lightness: enduring righteous deeds matter most, and perishable pleasures have no weight.

[BURSEVI:v10p386/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Both groups commit sins, though the first has fewer and outweighed sins and the second has many; the trial remains, so the Prophet tells ‘Ali to follow a bad deed with a good one, in keeping with God's forgiving name.
[BURSEVI:v10p386/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God's scale reverses ordinary scales: rising and elevation are heaviness, while falling is lightness; weighty deeds are enduring good works, and valueless light deeds are passing sensual pleasures.
[BURSEVI:v10p386/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Scales are light when a person has no good deed of weight or when sins outweigh good deeds.
[BURSEVI:v10p386/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Mas‘ud says one extra good deed leads to Paradise, while one extra bad deed leads to Hell.
[BURSEVI:v10p386/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | The inward reading makes the origin of those with light scales an abyss of veiling and a hot fire of ignorance, blindness, ego, passion, Satan, and the world.

[ALUSI:101:8/r1] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The scales are light because the person has no good deed of consequence, or because his evil deeds outweigh his good ones.

[CORPUSCORANICUM:111:3-5:kommentar/r5] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | Riddling that creates rhetorical tension also structures oath sequences such as Q 100 and teaching questions at 90:12–16, 97:2–4, 101:1–11, and 104:5–9. | mentions 100:1, 90:12, 90:13, 90:14, 90:15, 90:16, 97:2, 97:3, 97:4, 101:1, 101:2, 101:3, 101:4, 101:5, 101:6, 101:7, 101:8, 101:9, 101:10, 101:11, 104:5, 104:6, 104:7, 104:8, 104:9
